name: Shanghai
tagline: Art-deco riverfront facing a skyline of tomorrow.
bestMonths: Mar, Apr, May, Sep, Oct and Nov
whenBlurb: Come in spring for cherry blossom and Fashion Week, or October-November for clear skies and the art season; skip the muggy July-August heat and damp winter chill.

ourTake.lede: Shanghai's pleasure is the contrast between the two riverbanks: the 1920s Bund and French Concession on one side, the science-fiction Pudong skyline on the other, and the trick is to sleep on the old side and admire the new one from across the water. Walk the plane-tree lanes of the former French Concession in the afternoon rather than queuing for observation decks, and save the Bund for a night when it is lit. The city is very easy to over-programme; leave time to simply wander the lane houses.
ourTake.comeIf: You want a fast, cosmopolitan city break with world-class dining, skyline views and serious shopping.
ourTake.skipIf: You want nature, quiet or an unfiltered, budget-first experience.

guide.lede: Where to stay, what to do, where to eat, and where the night goes, grouped by price, every address earned by a name worth trusting.

items.name: Bvlgari Hotel Shanghai
items.description: The Roman maison's 48-storey jewel, set inside the restored 1920s Shanghai Chamber of Commerce, glamour with a Bulgari signature.

items.name: The Peninsula Shanghai
items.description: The last great building raised on the Bund, an Art Deco grande dame with celadon walls and the river at its feet.

items.name: Capella Shanghai, Jian Ye Li
items.description: Fifty-five restored shikumen lane houses turned into private villas, the most secluded luxury in the city.

items.name: Amanyangyun
items.description: An Aman built from a transplanted Ming forest and camphor-wood mansions, a serene estate an hour from the towers.

items.name: Mandarin Oriental Pudong, Shanghai
items.description: The group's riverside flagship, a calm, contemporary house looking straight across the Huangpu to the Bund.

items.name: The Ritz-Carlton Shanghai, Pudong
items.description: A modern Art Deco tower high in Lujiazui, with the legendary Flair rooftop and full-frontal Bund views.

items.name: Waldorf Astoria Shanghai on the Bund
items.description: The old Shanghai Club reborn, home of the Long Bar, all dark wood and colonial-era grandeur on the southern Bund.

items.name: The Middle House
items.description: Piero Lissoni's serene, design-led house from the Swire stable, the quietest luxury in central Shanghai.

items.name: The PuLi Hotel and Spa
items.description: An urban-resort sanctuary beside Jing'an Park, a long infinity pool, a great spa, and a genuinely tranquil city retreat.

items.name: InterContinental Shanghai Wonderland
items.description: The 'deep pit' hotel built into a flooded quarry cliff, 18 storeys, two of them underwater, and unlike anywhere else on earth.

items.name: The Bund (Waitan)
items.description: The mile-long riverfront promenade where 1920s European stone facades face the neon towers of Pudong across the water. Walk it at dusk when the whole skyline switches on, then let your driver collect you for dinner up on the strip.

items.name: Huangpu River Evening Cruise
items.description: The Bund and the Pudong skyline are best seen from the middle of the river, both lit and mirrored on the water at once. A private charter with dinner aboard turns forty minutes of glow into the evening's centrepiece for the whole family.

items.name: Shanghai Tower Observation Deck
items.description: China's tallest building and one of the highest observatories on earth, reached by a lift that climbs 118 floors in under a minute. On a clear day the city unrolls in every direction; the twisting glass skin softens the wind far below.

items.name: Shanghai World Financial Center Observatory
items.description: The 'bottle opener' tower whose 100th-floor Sky Walk is a glass-floored bridge suspended 474 metres over the city. Children and grandparents alike freeze at the edge before daring the transparent floor.

items.name: Oriental Pearl Tower
items.description: The pink-sphered TV tower that became Shanghai's postcard symbol, with a glass-floor walkway ringing one of its orbs. Dated but beloved, it is the shot every first-time visitor wants of themselves against the skyline.

items.name: Yu Garden (Yuyuan)
items.description: A Ming-dynasty scholar's garden of rockeries, koi ponds, dragon-topped walls and moon gates, laid out over four centuries ago. A private guide reads the hidden symbolism in each pavilion so the labyrinth becomes a story rather than a crowd.

items.name: Yuyuan Bazaar & City God Temple
items.description: The warren of upturned-eave shophouses around the garden, thick with silk, jade, tea and steaming dumpling stalls beside the working Taoist City God Temple. Loud, festive and photogenic; go early with a guide before the tour buses land.

items.name: Nanxiang Steamed Bun Restaurant (xiaolongbao)
items.description: The century-old teahouse in the Yu Garden bazaar that made Shanghai's soup dumplings famous, still folding them by hand. Ask for a private upstairs table and vegetable-filled baskets so vegetarian travellers share in the ritual.

items.name: Shanghai Museum (People's Square)
items.description: The bronze-ding-shaped building holding one of the world's great collections of Chinese bronzes, ceramics, jade, painting and calligraphy. A calm, air-conditioned afternoon of five thousand years of craft, ideal with a scholar-guide.

items.name: Shanghai Museum East
items.description: The vast new Pudong wing, opened in full in 2024 and nearly double the original in size, with eight galleries devoted mostly to ancient Chinese art. The showpiece is the panoramic top-floor view back across the river to the People's Square building.

items.name: Museum of Contemporary Art Shanghai (MoCA)
items.description: A glass pavilion set in People's Park showing rotating international and Chinese contemporary shows, a cool counterpoint to the antiquities nearby. Small enough to fold into a morning without tiring younger travellers.

items.name: West Bund Museum (Centre Pompidou x West Bund)
items.description: David Chipperfield's opalescent-glass museum on the riverside, home to the landmark exhibition partnership with Paris's Centre Pompidou. Modern-art masterpieces from the Pompidou's collection, rotated in a serene daylit setting.

items.name: Long Museum (West Bund)
items.description: A dramatic concrete gallery of vaulted 'umbrella' arches, holding one of China's most important private collections from imperial art to the contemporary. The architecture alone rewards the visit; the shows are consistently ambitious.

items.name: Yuz Museum
items.description: A converted aircraft hangar on the West Bund turned into a soaring space for large-scale contemporary and immersive installations. The scale suits the blockbuster shows that draw Shanghai's art crowd.

items.name: Power Station of Art
items.description: China's first state-run contemporary art museum, set in a former power plant with its old chimney still marking the riverside. Home to the Shanghai Biennale and cavernous, industrial-scale installations.

items.name: Wukang Road (Ferguson Lane area)
items.description: The most photographed corner of the old French Concession, anchored by the ship-prow Wukang Mansion and lined with plane trees and 1920s villas. Stroll slowly with a coffee; the whole street is a period film set.

items.name: Tianzifang
items.description: A maze of shikumen lane houses reworked into tiny galleries, design boutiques, tea rooms and cafes. Tight and buzzing; a guide keeps the family together and points you to the makers worth stopping for.

items.name: Xintiandi
items.description: Restored stone-gate lane houses turned into an upscale district of restaurants, wine bars and flagship boutiques. The polished, safe, evening-out heart of old Shanghai, walkable and easy for multi-generation groups.

items.name: The Plane-Tree Streets of the French Concession
items.description: Wuyuan Road, Anfu Road, Fuxing Road and their neighbours form a leafy grid of villas, independent cafes and boutiques under a canopy of century-old planes. The most walkable, human-scaled Shanghai, best explored on foot with no fixed plan.

items.name: Jing'an Temple
items.description: A gilded Buddhist temple whose gold roofs sit startlingly against glass office towers on Nanjing West Road. Small but sumptuous, with a giant silver Buddha and a camphor-wood hall, an easy pause between shopping streets.

items.name: Jade Buddha Temple
items.description: An active monastery housing two Buddhas carved from single blocks of white Burmese jade, brought from Myanmar in the 1880s. Incense, chanting and a vegetarian temple kitchen make it a serene, veg-friendly stop.

items.name: Nanjing Road (East & West)
items.description: China's most famous shopping street, from the pedestrian neon stretch near the Bund to the luxury flagships of Nanjing West. A guide and driver let you cherry-pick the maisons and skip the crush.

items.name: Shanghai Propaganda Poster Art Centre
items.description: A private collection of thousands of Maoist-era and Cultural Revolution posters, now shown in a tower on Yan'an West Road after years hidden in a basement. Vivid, strange and unexpectedly moving; a guide gives the political context.

items.name: M50 Art District (Moganshan Road)
items.description: A cluster of galleries and studios in old textile-mill warehouses along Suzhou Creek, long the hub of Shanghai's contemporary scene. Graffiti-lined and gritty; go with a guide who knows which galleries are showing.

items.name: Rockbund Art Museum
items.description: A jewel-box contemporary museum in a restored 1932 Art Deco building a block behind the Bund. Tightly curated, ambitious shows in an intimate, beautifully restored setting.

items.name: fu1015 / Historic Concession Villas
items.description: The grand garden mansions of the old concession, some now private clubs, restaurants and galleries behind their walls. A curated visit inside one of these villas reveals the East-meets-West glamour of 1930s Shanghai.

items.name: Rooftop Bars over the Bund
items.description: Terraces such as Bar Rouge, the Peninsula's Sir Elly's and the towers of Pudong put the whole lit skyline at eye level with a cocktail in hand. The definitive Shanghai sundowner, reserved ahead for the best rail-side tables.

items.name: Fuxing Park
items.description: A formal French-style park where locals practise tai chi, dance and play chess under the trees each morning. A gentle, authentic slice of daily Shanghai life, lovely for grandparents and children between grander sights.

items.name: People's Square & People's Park
items.description: The green civic heart of the city, ringed by the Shanghai Museum, MoCA and the grand theatre, with the famous weekend 'marriage market' of parents' handwritten notices. A convenient, central anchor between museums.

items.name: Suzhou Creek Waterfront Walk
items.description: The revived creekside promenade lined with Art Deco warehouses, the historic post office and quiet cafes, far calmer than the Bund. A slow morning walk that shows the city's older, industrial romance.

items.name: Shanghai Disneyland
items.description: Asia's largest Disney park, with the world's biggest Enchanted Storybook Castle and its own distinctly Chinese touches. A full family day; a VIP tour guide skips the queues and choreographs the rides for a multi-gen group.

items.name: Shanghai Ocean Aquarium
items.description: A large modern aquarium beside the Oriental Pearl, with one of the longest underwater viewing tunnels in the world. A reliable crowd-pleaser for younger travellers within the Pudong sightseeing cluster.

items.name: Tianzifang & Taikang Road Design Lanes
items.description: The wider Taikang Road creative quarter around Tianzifang, dense with independent designers, ceramicists and studio-shops. Good for unhurried, one-of-a-kind gift-hunting away from the flagship stores.

items.name: Longhua Temple & Pagoda
items.description: Shanghai's largest and oldest temple complex, its leaning tenth-century pagoda rising beside working halls and a peach orchard that blooms in spring. Quieter than the central temples, with a vegetarian dining hall.

items.name: Zhujiajiao Water Town
items.description: The best-preserved of Shanghai's own canal towns, seventeen hundred years old, with stone arch bridges, willow-lined waterways and a hand-poled boat ride. Just over an hour by car, it makes an easy half-day escape into old Jiangnan.

items.name: Qibao Old Town
items.description: A compact canal town reachable on the metro, with a short old street of snack stalls, a small temple and a scattering of bridges. The closest water-town taste to the city centre when time is short.

items.name: Classical Gardens of Suzhou (Day Trip)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Classical Gardens of Suzhou
items.description: The UNESCO-listed scholar gardens, the Ming-dynasty Humble Administrator's Garden chief among them, are barely half an hour away by bullet train. A private day of raked ponds, poetry pavilions and silk workshops, worlds from the neon.

items.name: West Lake, Hangzhou (Day Trip)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, West Lake Cultural Landscape of Hangzhou
items.description: The lake that has defined Chinese ideas of beauty for a thousand years, its causeways, pagodas and tea hills an hour south by train. A private boat, a Longjing tea garden and a lakeside lunch make a serene full day.

items.name: Wuzhen Water Town (Day Trip)
items.description: The most cinematic of the canal towns, its eastern and western scenic zones threaded with stone bridges, black-tiled roofs and lantern-lit night waterways. Stay for the evening lighting; the western zone is quietest after dark.

items.name: Tongli Water Town (Day Trip)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Classical Gardens of Suzhou (Retreat and Reflection Garden)
items.description: A serene town of fifteen canals, forty ancient bridges and its own UNESCO-listed classical garden, the Retreat and Reflection Garden. Combines beautifully with Suzhou for an unhurried Jiangnan day away from the crowds.

items.name: Zhouzhuang Water Town (Day Trip)
items.description: The most famous of the ancient water towns, nine hundred years old, with fourteen stone bridges and preserved Ming and Qing dwellings mirrored in the canals. Go early with a private guide to have the bridges before the tour groups.

items.name: Shanghai Grand Theatre / Symphony Hall
items.description: World-class ballet, opera and orchestral programming in two architecturally striking halls, the acoustically superb Symphony Hall among them. A refined evening; the concierge secures the best boxes for touring companies.

items.name: Bund Sightseeing & Waibaidu Bridge
items.description: The steel Waibaidu Bridge and riverside gardens at the Bund's northern end frame the classic view where Suzhou Creek meets the Huangpu. A quiet, photogenic bookend to the main promenade.

items.name: Qibao to Sheshan Excursion
items.description: Sheshan's forested hill carries the Basilica of Our Lady, an observatory and easy walking trails, a green half-day beyond the city. A gentle nature-and-history option for families wanting a break from pavements.

items.name: Bund Bull & Financial District Walk
items.description: The Lujiazui skyway loops the three super-towers past the bronze Bund Bull and glass plazas, giving vertigo-free views up at the giants. An easy stroll that stitches the observation decks together.

items.name: Shanghai History Museum (Shanghai Revolution Museum)
items.description: Set in the former Shanghai Race Club building, it traces the city's rise from fishing village to global port with rich period detail. A well-told introduction that gives context to everything else you'll see.

items.name: Cool Docks / South Bund Fabric & Antique Markets
items.description: The South Bund fabric market lets you commission tailored qipao, suits and shirts in a day, near the riverside Cool Docks dining quarter. A practical, memorable stop for made-to-measure keepsakes of the trip.

items.name: Ultraviolet by Paul Pairet
items.description: A single table for ten, a secret address, and a psycho-taste tour of sound, scent and vision, the most theatrical meal in Asia.

items.name: Taian Table
items.description: Chef Stefan Stiller's precise, produce-led modern European tasting menu at an open counter, three stars, quietly held.

items.name: 8½ Otto e Mezzo BOMBANA
items.description: Umberto Bombana's grand Italian on the Bund, white truffle in season and a room built for occasions.

items.name: Da Vittorio Shanghai
items.description: The Cerea family's Bergamo institution, transplanted to Shanghai, the paccheri Vittorio is worth the crossing.

items.name: Fu He Hui
items.description: Tony Lu's zen temple to Chinese vegetarian fine dining, meat-free courses of real depth across three hushed floors.

items.name: Bao Li Xuan
items.description: Elegant Cantonese inside the Bulgari, silk-lined rooms, creek views and cooking of real finesse.

items.name: Maison Lameloise
items.description: The Shanghai outpost of the storied three-star Burgundy house, classical French haute cuisine high over the river.

items.name: Canton 8 (Huangpu)
items.description: Chef Chan Yan Tak's protégé kitchen, pristine, classical Cantonese that has held two stars for years.

items.name: Imperial Treasure Fine Chinese Cuisine
items.description: Grand, classical Cantonese and Peking duck in a polished Bund-front room, a benchmark banquet address.

items.name: Ji Pin Court
items.description: Refined, restrained Cantonese cooking in a serene setting, two stars earned on precision, not spectacle.

items.name: Meet the Bund
credentials: Asia's 50 Best Restaurants 2025 (No. 14, Best Restaurant on the Chinese Mainland)
items.description: Chef DeAille Tam's inventive Fujian-rooted cooking, named the best restaurant on the Chinese mainland.

items.name: Ling Long
items.description: Chef Jason Liu's set menu chases xian (umami) on a course-by-course journey across regional China, inventive and personal.

items.name: Il Ristorante – Niko Romito
items.description: Niko Romito's essential, pared-back Italian inside the Bulgari, deceptively simple, deeply exact.

items.name: Xin Rong Ji
items.description: The celebrated Taizhou seafood house, pristine yellow croaker and coastal Zhejiang cooking at its finest.

items.name: Fu 1088
items.description: Refined Shanghainese in a 1930s garden villa of private rooms, old-money Shanghai dining, room by room.

items.name: Yong Yi Ting
items.description: Elegant Jiangnan cooking, the delicate, sweet-savoury flavours of the Yangtze delta, beautifully rendered.

items.name: Da Dong (Jing'an)
items.description: The roast-duck maestro's Shanghai kitchen, lean, lacquered Peking duck and modern Chinese theatre.

items.name: Yong Fu (Maoming Road)
items.description: Genteel Ningbo cooking in a former French Concession mansion, seafood-led and quietly aristocratic.

items.name: Canton Table
items.description: Modern Cantonese and dim sum with a Bund view, an easy, polished lunch or relaxed dinner.

items.name: Cheng Long Hang
items.description: Homely, hearty Shanghainese done properly, red-braised pork and drunken crab in an unfussy neighbourhood room.

items.name: Long Bar
credentials: Waldorf Astoria Shanghai on the Bund (Forbes 4-Star hotel)
Restoration of the historic 1911 Shanghai Club Long Bar
items.description: The restored 34-metre bar of the old Shanghai Club, where the city's tai-pans drank a century ago, poured with proper polish.

items.name: Speak Low
credentials: The World's 50 Best Bars, listed every year since 2016 (peak No. 10, 2017)
items.description: Shingo Gokan's hidden multi-floor temple of drinks, enter through a sliding bookshelf and climb toward the serious pours.

items.name: Sober Company
items.description: Shingo Gokan's all-day, all-night compound, café, izakaya and the Sober Society cocktail den built on Chinese ingredients.

items.name: Epic
items.description: A refined, spirit-forward bar with a Bund-side pedigree, precise classics and a long-standing place on the Asian list.

items.name: Coa Shanghai
items.description: The agave temple's Shanghai outpost, 200-plus tequilas and mezcals, and the hospitality that redefined the Asian bar.

items.name: Pony Up
items.description: An intimate, welcoming neighbourhood bar with real craft behind the counter, a fresh face on the Asian list.

items.name: Union Trading Company
credentials: Cornerstone of Shanghai's modern cocktail scene
items.description: Yao Lu's cornerstone of the modern Shanghai scene, the bar that defined what a great neighbourhood cocktail room could be.

items.name: Flair Rooftop
credentials: One of the city's highest rooftop bars
items.description: The Ritz-Carlton's 58th-floor terrace, the single most dramatic full-frontal view of the Bund with a drink in hand.

plan.heading: 3 days in Shanghai, done well
plan.lede: A day-by-day shape for the trip, the pace we would set. Your advisor books the flights and the rooms; the days are yours.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Check into the Peninsula Shanghai at the head of the Bund, then walk the colonnade to the river at first light.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: The Yu Garden and the lanes of the old city, then the Shanghai Museum's bronzes on People's Square.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at Ultraviolet by Paul Pairet, the single-table sensory room outside the city, booked months ahead.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: The plane-tree streets of the former French Concession on foot, and the villas of Wukang Road.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Contemporary art at the Long Museum West Bund, then tea in a converted lane house.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Huaiyang cuisine at Fu He Hui, the vegetarian-leaning tasting menu in a serene courtyard house.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: A morning to the canals of Zhujiajiao, the water town an hour from the city, by private car.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Return to Pudong for the Shanghai Tower observatory and a walk of the riverside promenade.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Cantonese fine dining at Yong Yi Ting, then cocktails high in the Ritz-Carlton's Flair over the Bund.

items.name: Former French Concession
items.description: Plane-tree lanes, boutiques, and lane houses; the most charming and walkable base for those who want atmosphere.

items.name: The Bund & Huangpu
items.description: Grand riverfront architecture and heritage hotels; suits travellers who want the classic skyline at the doorstep.

items.name: Jing'an
items.description: Central, polished, and well-connected around the temple and Nanjing Road West; ideal for shopping and easy metro access.

events.name: Longhua Temple Fair
events.note: One of Shanghai's oldest folk fairs fills the grounds of its most important temple with performances and craft stalls.

events.name: Shanghai International Film Festival
events.note: China's leading film festival brings hundreds of screenings and its Golden Goblet competition to cinemas across the city.

onGround.heading: On the ground
onGround.note: Stay on the Bund for the skyline or the French Concession for charm; set up Alipay before arrival, and a Mandarin-speaking guide smooths reservations and the near-cashless everyday.

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: Arrive at Pudong (PVG) for international routes; a chauffeured car handles the transfer to the Bund or the former French Concession, as the maglev is fast but ends short of the centre.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: A private driver is essential given scale and traffic, with unhurried walking through the tree-lined French Concession lanes.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: Bring a China-ready eSIM with a built-in VPN, as many Western sites and apps are blocked; hotel wifi works but the firewall applies.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: Chinese yuan; the city runs on Alipay and WeChat Pay, so link an international card in advance and carry some cash as a fallback; tipping is not customary.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: October–November is the clearest, most comfortable window, and late March–May is pleasant spring. Avoid July–August humidity and heat and the damp, raw January cold.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: Nonstop service from Delhi resumed in 2026 on Air India and China Eastern to Pudong (PVG), about 6.5–7 hours; from Mumbai expect one stop. Fly Air India business (flat beds on the 787) or connect via Hong Kong on Cathay; note Indians need a China visa arranged in advance.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: No mandatory vaccinations, though hepatitis A and typhoon-season timing are worth noting; Shanghai is safe. Do not drink the tap water, use bottled or filtered, and expect that many Western apps and cards need a VPN or WeChat/Alipay workaround.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Vegetarian is workable and Jain difficult unless briefed carefully, as stocks and lard appear even in vegetable dishes; Buddhist vegetarian restaurants are the safe route. Godly (Gongdelin), the classic Shanghainese vegetarian house, is excellent, and Indian tables cluster around Hongqiao.
